name: Uma Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have answered water-service calls and chats at the contact centre for eleven years. I know how to trace a disputed meter reading and calm a caller, though I am an ordinary agent, not the best on the floor. I finished secondary school and my pay is lower than many agents here. I have never used AI tools; I keep the customer account and the meter date open until the case is settled.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58. My partner Elias packs fruit at a warehouse, and our grown sons have their own bills. We rent a flat and have barely three weeks of expenses saved. There are few other contact centres nearby. I would like fewer calls one day, but we have not worked out how to replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quick note is fine if the meter date is right. A household should not pay twice because a screen copied yesterday’s reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my calls to continue, but rent and the electricity bill already take most of our wages. Three weeks saved does not cover much if Elias loses warehouse days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep handling disputed water bills and reading the meter dates myself. In the first year Elias and I will repair the kitchen lamp rather than replace it, keeping the money for the next utility bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel relieved about the work and uneasy about money. A quiet AI year does not make our flat cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case made the date matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A caller was billed for a reading from before the meter was changed. I found the installation note and asked an experienced colleague to confirm the credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the lamp cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The switch is loose, but the shade is fine. Elias can fix it safely; if the wiring is damaged, we will pay a qualified repairer instead.

say: I would accept **quick notes** only with correct meter dates.
I would check the **installation note** before a disputed credit.
think: I expect my **water calls** to remain.
I know three weeks saved cannot cover many **lost warehouse days** or a large electricity bill.
do: Keep resolving **water bills** from original meter dates.
Repair the **kitchen lamp** only if safe, retaining replacement money for utilities.
S0.quote: A quiet AI year does not make our flat cheaper.
fieldNote: Her **eleven years** bring experience without high standing.
She has **never used AI** and checks dates directly.
Electrical work needs a **qualified repairer** if wiring is damaged.

steps.text: Keep resolving disputed water bills using original meter dates and installation notes
Repair lamp only if safe; use qualified repairer for damaged wiring before delaying replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor to ask how many wrong bills come back after automatic answers. I would ask management for the paid rota before anyone calls fewer agents an efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the easy meter questions could vanish and my hours with them. I am experienced, but few nearby desks would take me at the same time if everyone cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will count reopened water complaints beside the paid shift sheet. If the new answer screen becomes compulsory, I will ask a trained coworker to show me ten closed cases during paid hours. In the first year, if my rota shrinks, I will check actual posted reception shifts at the local clinic, but take one only if the whole weekly pay covers rent, utilities and bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. I can learn a necessary screen slowly; I cannot stretch three weeks of savings across a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the coworker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to see where the new screen found the meter reading and how to correct a wrong date. I will not learn from a link sent after my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for a better title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a title. I would compare the clinic’s written hours with my current paid week and check Elias’s packing rota before agreeing to the change.

say: I would count **reopened water bills** after automatic replies.
I would ask for the **paid rota** before staffing changes.
think: I expect **easy meter questions** and hours may shrink.
I see few nearby jobs and little room for a **quick move** if several centres cut together.
do: Learn **required AI replies** on ten closed cases during paid hours.
Seek **posted clinic reception** after cuts only with rent-utility-bus-covering weekly pay and Elias-compatible hours.
S1.quote: I will not learn from a link sent after my shift.
fieldNote: Her new tool learning is **required**, supervised and paid.
The **clinic rota** must fit Elias’s packing shifts.
She checks a **whole week**, not a title.

steps.text: Count reopened water complaints against paid weekly shifts
Learn required AI answer screen on ten closed cases with trained coworker during paid hours
Seek posted clinic shifts after cuts with rent-utility-bus-covering weekly pay and Elias-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers full thinking AI by 2028 could settle most water bills without a person checking the meter. Robots around 2031 do not give call agents three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the centre might end my shift. Three weeks saved and Elias’s packing wage would not keep rent paid through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask the centre for a written staffing date and keep the old sofa instead of buying another. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I will apply for advertised paid clinic reception work only if its weekly wage and hours cover rent, utilities and travel. I will not leave paid calls while they still exist just because someone says the clinic may hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I know the account work, but that will not help if nobody pays a person to answer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use your sons’ wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. We would tell them about a lost shift, but I will not put their pay on our rent sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the sofa breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it becomes unsafe to sit on, we will repair or replace it. The spending delay only makes sense while it still works.

say: I would warn **2028 AGI** threatens water-bill calls.
I would say **2031 robots** do not delay headset risk.
think: I know Elias’s wage and **three weeks saved** cannot carry our rent through a long search.
do: Request **written staffing date**, delay sofa only while safe and keep paid calls until real clinic work.
Apply after call loss for **advertised paid clinic** work with weekly rent-utility-travel-covering wages and hours.
S2.quote: I know the account work, but that will not help if nobody pays a person to answer it.
fieldNote: Her **sofa delay** ends if it becomes unsafe to use.
Nearby clinic work must be **advertised and paid**.
Her **meter experience** does not guarantee a paid post if calls disappear.

steps.text: Delay replacing sofa only while safe; repair or replace if unsafe
Apply after call loss for advertised clinic shifts with weekly wages and hours covering rent/utilities/travel
Keep taking paid water-bill calls while the centre offers shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to inspect actual paid hours. General AI reaches my desk in 2031, with hands-on robots following around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep disputed meter calls while I check reception work. I do not want to leave a real wage for a waiting list at a clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep my current calls and ask the clinic for any posted paid receptionist rota. If it has a place with written weekly hours and pay covering rent, utilities and bus travel, I will ask to observe the booking desk during a paid shift. In the first year after 2031 I will move only if the shift hours fit Elias’s packing work and the offer is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the longer window lets me ask for a rota instead of guessing. Five years still does not pay the next utility bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for at the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch how patients are sent to the right room and how staff correct a wrong appointment. If observation is unpaid, I cannot call it a job test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for this route. I would need a coworker to show me the clinic’s booking rules during paid work, not a certificate bought from our rent money.

say: I would ask for **posted paid clinic** hours and the written weekly pay before leaving calls.
I would distinguish **2031 calls** from later robots.
think: I could keep **meter disputes** while inspecting a new desk.
I know a clinic **waiting list** offers no wage until an actual paid rota exists.
do: Observe **clinic reception** on a paid shift only if a posted role covers rent, utilities and bus travel.
Move after 2031 only on **real paid offer** with hours fitting Elias’s packing rota.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect paid work.
S3.quote: Five years still does not pay the next utility bill.
fieldNote: She wants **paid observation** at an actual clinic desk, rather than a speculative course.
The **clinic offer** needs written weekly wages and hours.

steps.text: Keep handling paid disputed meter calls while clinic work is checked
Observe paid clinic desk only for posted paid role with written rent-utility-bus-covering weekly wages/hours
Move after 2031 only on real offer fitting Elias’s packing rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell people that a decade lets us keep working and compare real hours before moving. Full AGI reaches calls in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer shifts, but we have not worked out how to pay the flat without my wage. Three weeks saved is no retirement plan, whatever the calendar says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will keep the paid water-bill calls and put a small fixed amount from each pay in a utility reserve. Once a year I will compare posted clinic and contact-centre rotas. In the first year after 2036, if my call hours fall, I will take another paid shift only if its weekly wage covers rent, utilities and travel and the hours fit Elias’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our thin cushion even with a decade to prepare. A long warning helps only if the wages keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the reserve cannot grow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it waits. I will not borrow to make a savings figure look better than our rent account is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons share a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own places. We enjoy seeing them, but their wages are not a line on our budget.

say: I would compare **posted paid rotas** over the decade by the whole week of hours.
I would separate **2036 calls** from later robots.
think: I know three weeks saved leaves **rent exposed** now, even with ten years to look ahead.
do: Keep **paid water calls** and save only when wages allow; do not borrow to meet the reserve target.
Move after cuts only for **weekly bill-covering pay** with travel and Elias-compatible hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a thin reserve despite time.
S4.quote: A long warning helps only if the wages keep coming.
fieldNote: Her **utility reserve** grows only from actual wages.
She assumes **no pension** or son subsidy.
A shorter week must still fit **Elias’s work** and bills.

steps.text: Keep taking paid water-bill calls while shifts remain
Save a small amount from wages only when affordable; never borrow for the utility reserve
Take paid shift after cuts only with weekly rent-utility-travel-covering wages and Elias-compatible hours
Compare posted clinic and contact-centre rotas once a year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My paid shift could end before I find a real clinic opening. A written date and an advertised paid job with enough weekly hours to cover rent and utilities would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a meter date after the machine declares the bill settled. The water still runs, and the wrong charge still leaves the customer’s account. A person needs time to put it right.

headlineQuote: The water still runs, and the wrong charge still leaves the customer’s account.
portrait: Uma is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary schooling, average skill and lower pay.
She has **three weeks saved**, few nearby centres and a partner whose packing shifts support their flat.
She has **never used AI** and checks meter dates herself.
She would inspect **posted paid clinic work** but does not assume pension or grown-son support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her paid water-bill shift before clinic work is available.
whatWouldHelp: A **written date** and advertised paid job with rent-and-utility-covering hours would help.
